ACL 2022Text generation · Human evaluation

How Do Seq2Seq Models Perform on End-to-End Data-to-Text Generation?

Xunjian Yin, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗Code ↗ACL Anthology ↗

A high generation score does not explain what a model gets wrong. Fine-grained human annotation reveals how copying, pre-training, and dataset structure affect data-to-text errors.

01 / The research question

Fluent text can put the right entity in the wrong role

The paper gives a compact example with two facts about Williamson County: its largest city is Round Rock, and its county seat is Georgetown. A generated description instead calls Georgetown the largest city. The output uses a real entity from the input and reads naturally, but assigns that entity to the wrong relation. This is precisely the kind of mistake that a surface-level overlap score can struggle to characterize.

The example also separates two problems. The largest-city statement distorts a supplied fact, while the county-seat relation is never expressed. Fixing the wrong city removes the first error without recovering the missing information. A single quality score cannot tell a developer which repair is needed. The study therefore asks human annotators to locate errors and explain their type and severity, giving each model an interpretable error profile.

03 / Inside the method

Faithfulness and content selection are distinct requirements

The adapted MQM framework distinguishes eight error types. Inaccuracy intrinsic distorts information that is present in the source; inaccuracy extrinsic introduces information absent from it. Addition has a narrower meaning here: unnecessary or irrelevant material copied from the source. It is therefore not synonymous with hallucination. Omission, polarity errors, duplication, word form, and word order complete the taxonomy. These distinctions matter especially for ToTTo, where only highlighted table content should be described.

Annotators mark error spans and choose minor, major, or critical severity. Error penalties depend on severity and span length, normalized by output word count; omissions receive a fixed length of one. The study samples 80 inputs from each of four datasets and generates outputs from all five model configurations, producing 1,600 texts for annotation. Each text receives two independent annotations. Annotators are not told which model produced the output, reducing the influence of expectations about pre-training or model size.

  1. 01

    Compare representative models

    Evaluate Transformer, a pointer-generator Transformer, T5-small, T5-base, and BART-base on E2E, WebNLG, WikiBio, and ToTTo.

  2. 02

    Annotate specific errors

    Use an adapted MQM framework with eight error types covering accuracy and fluency, rather than relying only on automatic scores.

  3. 03

    Analyze the contributing factors

    Compare error profiles across architectures, pre-training, model sizes, and dataset structures to identify useful techniques and remaining weaknesses.

04 / Reading the evidence

An architectural improvement can move errors between categories

  • 5 × 4

    Models and datasets

    The study compares five Seq2Seq configurations across four benchmarks, exposing error patterns that differ by model and input structure.

  • Copy trade-off

    Fewer omissions, some extra content

    Copying helps reduce omission and extrinsic inaccuracy, while sometimes increasing addition errors; pre-training and model size strongly affect overall quality.

Copying helps preserve source content, but can also pull in content that the requested description does not need. On ToTTo, the pointer-generator lowers the omission error score from 19.74 to 7.48 relative to Transformer, while the addition score rises from 4.38 to 11.01. Those values are weighted error scores, not percentages of sentences with an error. The result explains why copying can improve overall quality while still creating a specific content-selection problem.

BLEU is not dismissed as wholly useless: its broad trend often agrees with human evaluation. But the rankings can diverge. On E2E, T5-base scores lower BLEU than T5-small, 59.96 versus 62.88, while its human score is higher, 96.36 versus 86.04. Fine-grained annotation explains what an aggregate number leaves unresolved. The interactive example lets a reader annotate the paper’s Table 2 output and score it with the same severity weights and length normalization used for the study.

Read the abstract

With the rapid development of deep learning, Seq2Seq paradigm has become prevalent for end-to-end data-to-text generation, and the BLEU scores have been increasing in recent years. However, it is widely recognized that there is still a gap between the quality of the texts generated by models and the texts written by human. In order to better understand the ability of Seq2Seq models, evaluate their performance and analyze the results, we choose to use Multidimensional Quality Metric(MQM) to evaluate several representative Seq2Seq models on end-to-end data-to-text generation. We annotate the outputs of five models on four datasets with eight error types and find that 1) copy mechanism is helpful for the improvement in Omission and Inaccuracy Extrinsic errors but it increases other types of errors such as Addition; 2) pre-training techniques are highly effective, and pre-training strategy and model size are very significant; 3) the structure of the dataset also influences the model’s performance greatly; 4) some specific types of errors are generally challenging for seq2seq models.
